Shipmen
shĭp'mĕn
n. pl. (sailors; seamen; men whose trade is the working of a ship)
Old English scipmann, a ship-man. The Authorized Version distinguishes shipmen (the crew) from the master and owner of the ship.

Biblical Definition

Solomon had no seafaring tradition, so he borrowed one: “Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon” (1Ki 9:27), and the fleet at Eziongeber brought gold from Ophir. The other appearance is the shipwreck voyage of Acts 27, and it is a study in itself. The shipmen “deemed that they drew near to some country” at midnight (Act 27:27) and sounded twice; then, under colour of casting anchors out of the foreship, “the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship” in the boat (Act 27:30). Paul, a prisoner and no sailor, saw the manoeuvre for what it was and told the centurion, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved — and the soldiers cut the ropes and let the boat fall off. This is the same chapter in which God had already promised Paul by an angel that there should be no loss of any man's life. The promise was absolute; the means were not optional. God ordains the end and the means together, and Acts 27 is the plainest narrative illustration of that doctrine in the New Testament: a divine guarantee, and a command to keep the crew aboard, in the same night.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a shipman as a seaman or sailor — a term now little used except in the Scriptures.

expand to see more

SHIPMAN, n. A seaman or sailor.

The shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country. Acts xxvii.

SHIPMASTER, n. The captain, master or commander of a ship.

Key Scripture

1Ki 9:27 — "And Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon."

Act 27:30 — "And as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship, when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship,"

Act 27:31 — "Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved."

Modern Corruption

A promise of God is repeatedly treated as a reason to neglect the means He appointed, and Acts 27:31 is the standing refutation.

expand to see more

In Acts 27 God had spoken plainly. An angel had stood by Paul in the night saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee. Paul believed it and said so publicly: I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me. Then, a few verses later, when the sailors tried to slip away in the boat, the same Paul said, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. There is no contradiction, and the two verses together are one of the clearest lessons in Scripture on decree and means. God ordained that all would live; He also ordained that the crew would stay aboard, that the ropes would be cut, that men would eat before the wreck, and that those who could swim would swim. A fatalism that reasons from God's sovereignty to the neglect of appointed means is not Reformed doctrine but its counterfeit, and it appears everywhere: in the man who will not see a physician because God is able to heal, in the church that will not evangelise because the elect will be saved, in the believer who will not resist a temptation because he is kept by the power of God. The LBCF holds both hands: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and yet so as thereby no violence is offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'anshey 'oniyyot, men of ships; Greek nautes (G3492), a sailor; Greek kubernetes (G2942), the ship's master or steersman.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'oniyyah (H591) — a ship; Hiram's navy and the ship of Tarshish that Jonah found; 1 Kings 9:27, Jonah 1:3.

Greek nautes (G3492) — a sailor, a shipman; the crew of the Alexandrian corn ship in the Adria; Acts 27:27, 27:30, Revelation 18:17.

Greek kubernetes (G2942) — a steersman, the ship's master; whose counsel the centurion preferred to Paul's; Acts 27:11, Revelation 18:17.

Usage

"“Shipmen that had knowledge of the sea” — Hiram's crews lent to Solomon's navy."

"“The shipmen were about to flee out of the ship” — the manoeuvre a prisoner detected."

"“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — the promise, and the means."
